units.title: Living Things
units.blurb: What makes something alive, what every living thing needs, and things that were once alive.

topics.title: Living or Not Living?
topics.short: Living things grow, need food, water and air, and can make new living things like themselves. A rock or a toy car does none of these.
topics.trouble: Children often decide by movement: a car, a cloud or a fire "is alive" because it moves, while a tree or a seed "is not" because it stays still. The test is growing, needing food and water, and making more of its own kind, not moving.

topics.title: What Living Things Need
topics.short: Every living thing needs water, air, food (plants make their own) and a place to live with enough room.
topics.trouble: Children think plants need food from us or from the soil the way animals eat. Plants need water, air and light, and they make their own food in their leaves.

topics.title: Once Living: Logs, Leaves and Shells
topics.short: A fallen leaf, a log, a seashell and an apple core were part of living things once. A rock, a coin and a cloud never were.
topics.trouble: Children sort a dry leaf or a log as "never living" because it no longer grows. Things that came from a living thing, like wood, cotton or a shell, are once living.

topics.title: Living Things Grow and Change
topics.short: A kitten grows into a cat and a seed grows into a tree. Living things start small and grow, and many change shape as they grow.
topics.trouble: Children think young living things are just smaller copies that only get bigger. Many change too: a seedling has fewer leaves than the plant it becomes, and a tadpole looks nothing like a frog.

topics.title: What Plants Need
topics.short: Plants need light, water, air, room to grow and nutrients from the soil. Without light or water, a plant wilts and can die.
topics.trouble: Children say plants get their food from the soil. Soil gives water and a few nutrients, but a plant makes its food in its leaves using light, air and water.

topics.title: Parts of a Plant
topics.short: Most plants have roots, a stem, leaves and, at some time, flowers. Each part has its own job.
topics.trouble: Children leave out the roots because they cannot see them, or think a tree is not a plant because it is big and woody. A tree has roots, a stem (the trunk), leaves and flowers too.

topics.title: What Roots Do
topics.short: Roots hold a plant in the ground and take in water and nutrients from the soil.
topics.trouble: Children think roots are only for holding the plant up, or that a plant drinks through its leaves. Most of a plant's water comes in through its roots.

topics.title: What Stems and Leaves Do
topics.short: The stem holds the plant up and carries water from the roots to the leaves. Leaves catch sunlight and make the plant's food.
topics.trouble: Children think the stem is just a stick with no job. It holds the leaves up to the light and is the pipe that carries water up and food down.

topics.title: Flowers, Fruits and Seeds
topics.short: Flowers make seeds. A fruit is the part of a plant that holds the seeds, so apples, tomatoes, peppers and pumpkins are all fruits.
topics.trouble: Children call only sweet foods fruits. To a scientist, a tomato, a cucumber and a pea pod are fruits because they hold seeds.

topics.title: Bees, Butterflies and Pollen
topics.short: Bees, butterflies, birds and the wind carry pollen from flower to flower, and that helps flowers make seeds.
topics.trouble: Children think bees visit flowers only to get food for themselves. They do, and while they drink nectar, pollen sticks to them and travels to the next flower, which helps the plant make seeds.

topics.title: How Seeds Travel
topics.short: Seeds travel away from their parent plant: blown by the wind, carried by water, stuck to fur, eaten in fruit by animals, or popped out of a pod.
topics.trouble: Children think every seed simply drops below its parent. Most plants spread their seeds farther away, where a new plant has room and light.

topics.title: A Seed Starts to Grow
topics.short: A seed holds a tiny plant and food for it. With water and warmth, it sprouts: a root grows down and a shoot grows up toward the light.
topics.trouble: Children think a seed needs sunlight to sprout. Most seeds sprout in the dark soil, using the food stored inside them; the young plant needs light once its first leaves come up.

topics.title: The Life Cycle of a Plant
topics.short: Seed, sprout, young plant, adult plant with flowers, then fruit with new seeds, and the cycle starts again.
topics.trouble: Children put the flower before the young plant, or forget that the cycle comes back around to seeds.

topics.title: Plants Make Their Own Food
topics.short: Green leaves use sunlight, air and water to make sugar, the plant's food. Animals cannot do this; they must eat.
topics.trouble: Children think a plant eats soil, so a big tree must have used up a lot of dirt. A tree is built mostly from air (carbon dioxide) and water, put together using the energy of sunlight.

topics.title: Plant Parts We Eat
topics.short: We eat roots (carrots), stems (potatoes), leaves (lettuce), flowers (broccoli), fruits (apples) and seeds (peas and corn).
topics.trouble: Children think a potato is a root; it is a swollen underground stem. They also call every vegetable a root or a leaf without asking which part it came from (a celery stick, for example, is the stalk of a leaf).

topics.title: What Animals Need
topics.short: Animals need food, water, air and shelter, a safe place to rest and raise their young.
topics.trouble: Children think only land animals need air. Fish need air too: they take the oxygen dissolved in water through their gills.

topics.title: Plant-Eaters, Meat-Eaters and Both
topics.short: Herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat other animals, and omnivores eat both.
topics.trouble: Children think all big or fierce-looking animals eat meat. Elephants, gorillas and cows are big plant-eaters, and a bear eats berries as well as fish.

topics.title: Body Parts That Help
topics.short: Beaks, claws, fins, wings, tails and teeth each help an animal get food, move or stay safe.
topics.trouble: Children think every bird beak or animal tooth is the same. The shape tells you the job: a hooked beak tears meat, a long thin beak sips nectar, flat teeth grind plants.

topics.title: Fur, Feathers, Scales and Skin
topics.short: Mammals have hair or fur, birds have feathers, fish and reptiles have scales, and amphibians have smooth, moist skin.
topics.trouble: Children think snakes are slimy. Snakes have dry scales; it is frogs and other amphibians that have moist skin.

topics.title: How Animals Move
topics.short: Animals walk, run, hop, fly, swim, crawl and slither, and their bodies are shaped for the way they move.
topics.trouble: Children think anything with wings flies and anything in water swims the same way. Penguins have wings but swim with them, and a whale moves its tail up and down while a fish moves its tail side to side.

topics.title: Young Animals and Their Parents
topics.short: Many young animals look like their parents; others look very different at first. Many parents feed and protect their young.
topics.trouble: Children think young always look like small copies of their parents. A caterpillar, a tadpole and a chick in down look quite different from the adults they become.

topics.title: Mammals
topics.short: Mammals have hair or fur, breathe air, and feed their babies milk. Dogs, mice, people, bats and whales are mammals.
topics.trouble: Children think a whale or a dolphin is a fish because it lives in water, and a bat is a bird because it flies. Both are mammals: they have hair, breathe air and feed their young milk.

topics.title: Birds
topics.short: Birds have feathers, a beak and two legs, and they hatch from eggs with hard shells. Not every bird can fly.
topics.trouble: Children think anything that flies is a bird and that penguins and ostriches are not birds. Feathers make a bird a bird; bats and bees fly but have none.

topics.title: Fish
topics.short: Fish live in water, breathe with gills, swim with fins, and most have scales.
topics.trouble: Children call every water animal a fish: whales, dolphins, jellyfish, starfish and crabs. A fish has gills, fins and a backbone.

topics.title: Reptiles
topics.short: Reptiles have dry, scaly skin and breathe air. Snakes, lizards, turtles and crocodiles are reptiles, and most hatch from eggs laid on land.
topics.trouble: Children think turtles are amphibians because some live in water. Turtles have dry scales and breathe air with lungs all their lives, so they are reptiles.

topics.title: Amphibians
topics.short: Amphibians have smooth, moist skin. Most start life in water with gills and live on land as adults. Frogs, toads and salamanders are amphibians.
topics.trouble: Children think a salamander is a lizard. A salamander has moist skin with no scales, so it is an amphibian; a lizard has dry scales, so it is a reptile.

topics.title: Insects
topics.short: Insects have six legs and three body parts, and many have wings. Ants, bees, beetles and butterflies are insects; spiders are not.
topics.trouble: Children call every small crawling animal a bug or an insect. Spiders have eight legs and two body parts, and worms have no legs at all, so neither is an insect.

topics.title: Sorting Animals into Groups
topics.short: Look for clues, such as fur, feathers, scales, moist skin, gills or six legs, to put an animal in its group.
topics.trouble: Children sort by where an animal lives or how it moves (everything in water is a fish, everything that flies is a bird). Body clues decide the group, not the home.

topics.title: What Is a Habitat?
topics.short: A habitat is the place where a plant or animal lives and finds the food, water and shelter it needs.
topics.trouble: Children think a habitat is just a house, like a nest or a burrow. A habitat is the whole place: the pond, the forest or the desert, with everything the animal uses there.

topics.title: Forests, Grasslands, Deserts and Icy Places
topics.short: Forests have many trees, grasslands are wide and grassy, deserts get very little rain, and polar places are cold and icy. Each has its own plants and animals.
topics.trouble: Children think deserts are always hot and empty of life. Many deserts are cold at night or in winter, and cactuses, lizards, snakes and kangaroo rats live there.

topics.title: Ponds, Rivers and Oceans
topics.short: Ponds and lakes hold still fresh water, rivers flow, and oceans are salty. Different plants and animals live in each.
topics.trouble: Children think all water is the same home, so an ocean fish could live in a pond. Most ocean animals need salty water and most pond animals need fresh water.

topics.title: Made for Their Home
topics.short: A polar bear's thick fur, a camel's wide feet and a cactus's spines all help them live where they live.
topics.trouble: Children think an animal could live anywhere if it moved there. A polar bear would overheat in a desert and a cactus would rot in a swamp; living things are suited to their own habitats.

topics.title: Animal Homes
topics.short: Birds build nests, bees build hives, rabbits dig burrows, spiders spin webs and beavers build lodges.
topics.trouble: Children think every animal lives in a nest. Each kind of animal makes or finds its own kind of shelter, and some, like many fish, have none at all.

topics.title: Living Things Change Their Surroundings
topics.short: Beavers dam streams, squirrels bury nuts that grow into trees, roots crack sidewalks, and people build roads and plant gardens.
topics.trouble: Children think only people change the land. Animals and plants change it too, a little at a time, as they meet their needs.

topics.title: Energy Starts with the Sun
topics.short: Plants use sunlight to make food. Animals get their energy by eating plants, or by eating animals that ate plants.
topics.trouble: Children think the sun gives animals energy by warming them, or that animals make their own food like plants. Animal energy comes from food, and that energy came from the sun through plants.

topics.title: Food Chains
topics.short: A food chain shows who eats whom: grass, then a rabbit, then a fox. Each arrow points from the food to the animal that eats it.
topics.trouble: Children draw the arrows backward, from the eater to the food ("the fox eats the rabbit"). The arrow shows where the energy goes: from the rabbit into the fox.

topics.title: Producers and Consumers
topics.short: Plants are producers because they make food. Animals are consumers because they eat to get their food.
topics.trouble: Children call a big animal at the top of a chain the producer because it is strongest. Producers are the plants at the start of every chain.

topics.title: Decomposers
topics.short: Worms, mushrooms and tiny bacteria break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil.
topics.trouble: Children think dead leaves and logs just disappear by themselves. Decomposers eat them, and that puts nutrients back into the soil for new plants.

topics.title: The Life Cycle of a Butterfly
topics.short: A butterfly starts as a tiny egg, hatches as a caterpillar, makes a chrysalis, and comes out as a butterfly.
topics.trouble: Children think the caterpillar and the butterfly are two different animals, or that the butterfly grows bigger after it comes out. It is one animal; it does all its growing as a caterpillar.

topics.title: The Life Cycle of a Frog
topics.short: A frog starts as an egg in the water, hatches as a tadpole with a tail and gills, grows legs, loses its tail, and becomes a frog.
topics.trouble: Children think tadpoles are tiny fish. A tadpole is a young frog: it grows legs, its tail shrinks away, and it starts breathing air.

topics.title: The Life Cycle of a Chicken
topics.short: A chick grows inside an egg, hatches, grows feathers as a young chicken, and becomes a grown hen or rooster.
topics.trouble: Children think chicks hatch with grown-up feathers, or that a chick is a different kind of bird. A chick grows in its egg for about three weeks, hatches covered in soft down, and grows feathers over several weeks.

topics.title: Comparing Life Cycles
topics.short: Some young look like small adults and just grow (a chick, a kitten); others change shape completely as they grow (a butterfly, a frog).
topics.trouble: Children think every animal has the same number of stages. A butterfly has four very different stages, a frog changes slowly, and a chick just grows.

topics.title: Our Five Senses
topics.short: We see with our eyes, hear with our ears, smell with our nose, taste with our tongue and feel with our skin.
topics.trouble: Children think we taste only with the tongue and that smell has nothing to do with it. Our nose helps us taste; food tastes flat when a cold blocks the nose.

topics.title: How Animals Use Their Senses
topics.short: An owl's big eyes see at night, a dog's nose follows smells, a bat hears echoes, and a cat's whiskers feel the way.
topics.trouble: Children think animals sense the world just as we do. Many animals see, hear or smell things we cannot, and each sense helps them find food and stay safe.

topics.title: Observing Like a Scientist
topics.short: Scientists use their senses and tools like a magnifying glass and a ruler to observe. An observation is what you notice; a guess is what you think might be true.
topics.trouble: Children mix observations with guesses or feelings ("the bug is sad"). An observation is something you can see, hear, smell or measure, like "the bug has six legs".

topics.title: Trees Through the Seasons
topics.short: Many trees grow new leaves in spring, are full and green in summer, turn colors and drop leaves in fall, and stand bare in winter. Evergreens keep their needles.
topics.trouble: Children think trees die in winter because they are bare. They are resting; the buds for next spring's leaves are already on the branches.

topics.title: Animals in Winter
topics.short: In winter some animals migrate to warmer places, some hibernate, and others stay active with thick fur and stored food.
topics.trouble: Children think every animal sleeps all winter. Most stay active, many birds fly away, and only some, like woodchucks and some bats, truly hibernate.

topics.title: Getting Ready for Winter
topics.short: In fall, squirrels store nuts, birds gather to fly south, and many animals grow thicker coats or eat extra food.
topics.trouble: Children think animals are surprised by winter. Many start getting ready in late summer and fall, when days get shorter and food is still easy to find.

topics.title: Caring for a Pet
topics.short: A pet needs food, fresh water, a clean home, exercise, gentle hands and visits to the vet.
topics.trouble: Children think a pet needs care only when they feel like playing with it. A pet needs food and fresh water every day, even on busy days.

topics.title: Caring for a Plant
topics.short: A potted plant needs the right amount of water (not too much), light, a pot with holes for drainage, and room to grow.
topics.trouble: Children think more water is always better. Too much water can drown the roots; most potted plants want the soil to dry a little between waterings.

topics.title: Caring for Nature
topics.short: Watch wild animals without touching or chasing them, leave nests alone, put rocks back the way you found them, and keep trash out of nature.
topics.trouble: Children think a baby bird alone on the ground needs to be picked up and taken home, or that a rock is just a rock. The rock is someone's roof, and parents of young birds are often nearby; tell a grown-up instead.
